## Proof

**Claim.** Yes. For every ideal $I$ of a Noetherian ring $R$, there exists a positive integer $n$ with $(\sqrt{I})^n \subseteq I$.

**Proof.**

Since $R$ is Noetherian, every ideal of $R$ is finitely generated. In particular the radical
$$\sqrt{I} = \{x \in R : x^k \in I \text{ for some } k \geq 1\}$$
is an ideal of $R$, hence finitely generated. Write
$$\sqrt{I} = (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_m)$$
for some $a_1, \ldots, a_m \in R$.

Because each generator $a_i$ lies in $\sqrt{I}$, by definition of the radical there exists an integer $k_i \geq 1$ such that
$$a_i^{k_i} \in I, \qquad i = 1, \ldots, m.$$
Set $k := \max(k_1, \ldots, k_m)$, so that $a_i^k \in I$ for every $i$.

Now set
$$n := m(k-1) + 1.$$
We show $(\sqrt{I})^n \subseteq I$.

A general element of $(\sqrt{I})^n$ is a finite sum of products $x_1 x_2 \cdots x_n$ with each $x_j \in \sqrt{I}$. Since $(\sqrt{I})^n$ is generated (as an $R$-module) by products of $n$ generators, it suffices to show that every product of the form
$$a_{i_1} a_{i_2} \cdots a_{i_n}, \qquad i_1, \ldots, i_n \in \{1, \ldots, m\},$$
lies in $I$; for then any $R$-linear combination of such products also lies in $I$.

Consider such a monomial $a_{i_1} \cdots a_{i_n}$. Among the $n$ factors, each factor is one of $a_1, \ldots, a_m$. By the pigeonhole principle, since $n = m(k-1)+1 > m(k-1)$, at least one generator $a_{i^\ast}$ occurs at least $k$ times among $i_1, \ldots, i_n$. (If every generator occurred at most $k-1$ times, the total number of factors would be at most $m(k-1) < n$, a contradiction.)

Therefore we may reorder the factors (the ring is commutative) and write
$$a_{i_1} \cdots a_{i_n} = a_{i^\ast}^k \cdot \Bigl(\text{product of the remaining } n-k \text{ factors}\Bigr).$$
Since $a_{i^\ast}^k \in I$ by construction, and $I$ is an ideal, the entire product lies in $I$.

Thus every generator of $(\sqrt{I})^n$ lies in $I$, so $(\sqrt{I})^n \subseteq I$. $\blacksquare$

**Remark.** The Noetherian hypothesis is essential: it guarantees finite generation of $\sqrt{I}$, which is what makes the pigeonhole argument close. In a non-Noetherian ring the radical of an ideal need not be finitely generated, and indeed one can construct ideals $I$ in non-Noetherian rings for which no power of $\sqrt{I}$ is contained in $I$.

### PROOF COMPLETE
